title: Organizations that report bonuses most often, and what pay may depend on
question: Which City-paid organizations report bonuses year after year, and do their returns say that anyone’s pay depended on revenue or on net earnings?
finding: 132 organizations reported at least one bonus from their own funds; 35 did so on every return on file (three or more). 38 of the 132 did so in a year when the City supplied a quarter or more of their revenue, and 5 of those on every return: Low Income Investment Fund, Main Street Launch, San Francisco Aids Foundation, Project Open Hand and Family Caregiver Alliance. On the form’s questions about how pay is set, 4 organizations answered yes in at least one year to pay that depends on revenue (10 returns), 2 to pay that depends on net earnings (3 returns) and 64 to payments not fixed in advance (177 returns). Among organizations with a bonus on file, those answering yes on revenue or net earnings are Delta Dental Plan of California, California Academy of Sciences, SF Community Clinic Consortium, Caremessage and Flourish Agenda, Inc.
how: For each organization: the number of tax years with a bonus from its own funds on the compensation schedule, out of the returns that carry the schedule; the number of payments; the largest and to whom. Three columns give the tax years in which the return answered yes on Schedule J, Part I, to line 5 (pay contingent on the revenues of the organization or a related one), the question after it (pay contingent on net earnings) and line 7 (any payments not fixed in advance). Organizations that paid a bonus in a year when the City supplied a quarter or more of their revenue come first; within each group the ranking is by years with a bonus, then by payments. The City share is from the latest return. Where the organization’s tax number was matched by hand and has not been verified, the last column says so.
limits: Paying a bonus every year is common where an incentive plan is part of the pay package, and the form asks about contingent pay precisely so that it is disclosed. Pay tied to revenue is usual for staff who bring in fees or gifts and for clinicians paid by productivity; the return’s explanation, which is linked, usually says who and why. What the tax rules forbid is pay that is unreasonable, not pay that varies. The compensation schedule (Schedule J) follows from the return’s question whether any listed person was paid more than $150,000, so bonuses to people below that line, and at organizations where nobody reaches it, are not on any return. The bonus column is defined by the tax form as bonus and incentive pay; organizations differ in what they put there, and some record a retention payment, a signing payment or a payout under a long-term plan in it.
